description: We are Healers of the Galaxy, an interdisciplinary team uniting medicine, chemistry, and computer systems to protect health in space missions. We combine clinical judgment (physiology and prevention), biochemical analysis (biomarkers and open data), and software development (intuitive UX/UI, data analysis, and autonomous systems) to transform complex data into clear, accessible solutions in critical environments.
summary: Heal-OS is an autonomous medical monitoring and assistance system designed for astronauts on long-duration missions, and adaptable for those who work or live far from a doctor: expeditions, offshore platforms, polar stations, and isolated communities. It combines continuous monitoring of vital signs (heart rate, oxygen saturation, estimated systolic blood pressure, skin temperature, and respiratory rate) with an interactive symptom self-assessment using a 3D model of the body. The system cross-references the user’s reports with their physiology, the spacecraft environment, and the mission phase, and returns probable causes, an alert level, and step-by-step guidance. It features a configurable medication database based on the mission’s first-aid kit and visual alerts that notify the crew. The goal is to reduce reliance on communication with Earth. It is a triage support tool, not a diagnostic tool.
details:
What does Heal-OS do?

Heal-OS monitors each crew member's vital signs and compares them to their own baseline to detect deviations early on. All crew members are displayed on the screen along with their status.

When someone feels discomfort, they select the area where it hurts on a 3D model (in the demo: frontal, retro-orbital, or occipital). The system applies a two-step protocol:

  1. Ruling out emergencies. A brief questionnaire checks for warning signs. If any warning signs appear, a red alert is triggered, the crew is notified, the alert is logged for Mission Control, and immediate stabilization steps are displayed.
  2. Probable causes. If there is no emergency, the questions are tailored to the affected area, and the system cross-references the answers with biometric data, the cabin environment (e.g., CO₂ levels), and the mission phase.

The result is a guided plan: prioritized probable causes, alert level, a checklist with timers, and initial management recommendations based on the first-aid kit’s supplies. Everything is recorded in a medical log

How does it work?

On missions to the Moon and Mars, the crew will not be able to rely on mission control: on Mars, one-way communication can take up to 20 minutes(nasa.gov/hrp/hazard-distance-from-earth/)

NASA identifies five health risks: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravitational fields, and closed and hostile environments (nasa.gov/hrp/hazards). Heal-OS offers autonomous triage: it provides guidance on what might be happening to an astronaut and what to do, without a doctor or an internet connection. The same logic applies on Earth for anyone who works or lives far from medical help.

  1. 3D anatomical selection. The user taps the model, and the system maps the area to a clinical region. Depending on the area, the questionnaire adapts and is limited to about 5 to 7 questions that do not require typing.
  2. An inference engine that cross-references 4 sources: Each decision combines user input, biometric telemetry, environmental telemetry (CO₂, O₂, pressure, noise, and temperature), and the active phase or profile (microgravity, ascent, surface, or Earth). Each vital sign is compared to the crew member’s own baseline, not to general averages. In addition, the environment is assessed before attributing the symptom to the body: a headache accompanied by elevated CO₂ is treated first as an air-related problem.
  3. Hierarchical rules based on severity. The rules are evaluated at three levels: life-threatening red flags, environmental and phase-related causes, and internal status. If a critical rule is triggered, the questionnaire is terminated and action is taken immediately. Currently, there are [N] rules for the head.
  4. NASA-STD-3001 Alert Code. The levels RED, YELLOW, and NORMAL are used (Appendix F.6.4). Red is reserved for life-threatening situations. Follow-up (reassess in X minutes, contact a physician, confirm with instruments) is managed using specific indicators, without introducing new colors. An alert that worsens escalates in two steps and does not jump directly to red.
  5. Graceful degradation in the event of signal loss: If a sensor loses connection (***) or its data becomes outdated, the system does not block the decision: it issues a partial hypothesis and sets a manual measurement as the first step. When symptoms are consistent with a red flag and critical data is missing, it chooses the conservative option. It also recognizes the limitations of the sensors (skin temperature is not core temperature, and blood pressure is a systolic estimate) and requests confirmation with a clinical thermometer or blood pressure cuff.
  6. Configurable rules: Each rule follows the format IF [user + biometrics + environment + phase] THEN [hypothesis + level + actions], with thresholds that can be edited by profile (the acceptable CO₂ level in a space station is higher than on Earth [add source]). A flight physician can adjust them without reprogramming the system.
  7. Notification and Log: Every alert generates a notification and a log entry containing the time, zone, responses, telemetry at the time, the rule that triggered the alert, and the actions taken. If there is no link to Earth, the message is queued and sent as soon as the connection is reestablished. In the meantime, Heal-OS guides the crew on board using the defined rules of action, without waiting for a response.
  8. Configurable medication database. Initial treatment recommendations are tailored to the contents of the mission’s first-aid kit: available medications, indications, and contraindications. [In this MVP, a sample list using publicly available information is used, intended to be replaced by the mission’s official form.]
  9. A single system for space and Earth. With adaptive profiles (microgravity, the surface of Mars, high-risk work, everyday health), the same logic applies to a lunar mission or a remote construction site.

Data and Scope

The system variables correspond to those of real devices: Bio-Monitor (vital signs) (asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/sciences/bio-monitor.asp), Actiwatch (sleep) (nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/wearable-tech-for-space-station-research/), and environmental sensors such as the MCA, CDM, and CSA-CP (cabin air, CO₂, and toxic gases (nasa.gov/reference/environmental-control-and-life-support-systems-eclss/)). In this MVP, the values are simulated. Heal-OS is a triage support tool, not a diagnostic tool, and its thresholds are pending validation by physicians, ideally those specializing in aerospace medicine.

Project vision

Extend the system to the entire body, connect it to real hardware, and prepare it for long trips, where average battery life is critical.

What are the benefits?

  • Early detection and standardized response. An initial triage protocol for acute symptoms—such as severe headaches or neurological abnormalities—identifies warning signs and guides the response using defined decision trees, thereby reducing the need for improvisation in stressful situations.
  • Autonomy in scenarios with communication delays. When contact with mission control is delayed or interrupted, the system guides the initial stabilization steps using interactive checklists. It logs the report to be sent once communication is restored and continues to provide on-board assistance in the meantime.
  • Reduced cognitive load. An interactive body model and branching questionnaires allow users to report a medical condition with just a few taps, even when experiencing pain or fatigue. The visual distinction between red alerts and wellness recommendations is designed to ensure that each step is clear.
  • Continuous monitoring and traceability. The biometric sensor passively monitors vital signs and detects deviations from the personal baseline. The logbook maintains a history of events for each crew member, which is useful for medical follow-up during and after the mission.

Expected impact

  • Operational and safety. By enabling early intervention and autonomous decision-making in the event of communication delays, Heal-OS aims to help reduce the need for emergency medical evacuations and give the crew greater clinical independence.
  • Human-Centered and Preventive. The combination of continuous biometric monitoring and guided reports aims to shift from reactive to proactive and personalized medicine, helping to detect early signs of cumulative wear and tear caused by fatigue, stress, or microgravity.
  • Transfer to Earth. Its modular architecture can be applied in isolated communities, polar stations, offshore platforms, and rural areas with limited access to specialists, bringing safe triage protocols and timely stabilization within reach.

Creative Process

During the creative process, as a team we sought to develop a solution that would allow us to monitor and care for astronauts’ health when they do not have immediate access to a doctor.

To that end, we conceived of Heal-OS as a system that not only records vital signs but also analyzes symptoms, environmental conditions, and the stage of the mission to detect potential health issues.

In addition, we incorporated the idea of a 3D body model that allows users to indicate where they feel pain and answer specific questions. The system would also compare vital signs with each person’s typical values, taking into account the physical changes caused by the space environment, such as microgravity and sleep disturbances.

We also aim for it to function in the event of sensor failures, request manual measurements when necessary, and generate alerts based on the severity of each situation.

Finally, we believe that Heal-OS should operate autonomously, without relying on a constant connection to Earth, and that it should be adaptable to other isolated environments where access to medical care is limited.

Thus, we aim to create a comprehensive, autonomous, and adaptable tool that prioritizes people’s health and safety.

Tools, programming languages, hardware, and software used for development

Graphical User Interface (GUI) Design

To ensure safe operation in environments characterized by isolation and fatigue, the Heal-OS interface is based on the human factors engineering requirements of NASA-STD-3001, Volume 2—Section 10.0 (Crew Interfaces) and Appendix F (Display Standard). Rather than dividing the workflow across multiple screens—which could disorient the operator—a single-screen situational awareness architecture was adopted, organized into five fixed modules: a top context bar, a crew selector, a layered 3D anatomical viewer, a continuous telemetry monitor, and a dynamic triage panel.

Visual and Readability Criteria (Appendix F.5)

  • Unambiguous Typography (F.5.1): Use of clean sans-serif fonts and tabular/monospaced typography for clocks and metrics to avoid visual confusion between similar characters (0 vs. O, 1 vs. l).
  • Extreme Contrast (F.5.2): A matte dark color scheme that ensures a minimum contrast ratio of 6:1 (target 10:1, exceeding the WCAG 2.1 AAA standard) to maintain readability in low light or when reflections occur in the cockpit.
  • Dual Coding (F.5.2): Color is never the sole channel of information; each status or alert combines a color code, explicit iconography, and a text label.

Data Display Rules (Section 10.2.1 and Appendix F.4 / F.5.6)

  • Data Overflow Prevention (F.4): No critical numbers or text are truncated with ellipses (...). If a value exceeds the width of its container, each character is replaced with yellow asterisks (***) to prevent partial readings.
  • Display of Stale or No-Signal Data ([V2 10020]): Disconnected parameters are visually represented by *** in amber yellow and the timestamp of the last valid data point, preventing the display of 0 or frozen values without warning.
  • Standardized Units (F.5.6): Each measurement permanently displays its unit (BPM, RPM, mmHg, °C, mSv, %) and clarifies the type of measurement when there is an instrumental limitation (e.g., skin temperature).

Interaction, Alerts, and Error Prevention (Sections 10.3–10.4 and Appendices F.4–F.6)

  • Tiempo estándar y ventanas no intrusivas (F.6.1 / F.4): El reloj de Tiempo Transcurrido de Misión (MET) permanece visible en todo momento. Los paneles secundarios o modales son cerrables y nunca ocultan los signos vitales críticos.
  • Control de parpadeos y alarmas (F.4): Las señales intermitentes están sincronizadas sin afectar la lectura del texto, e incorporan un botón accesible para silenciar la alerta tras 10 segundos conservando su registro visual.
  • Protección en acciones críticas (F.4): Los botones de comandos irreversibles o reportes de emergencia incorporan confirmación explícita y bordes de seguridad diagonales negros y amarillos (hazard borders) para evitar pulsaciones accidentales.
  • Formularios y checklists de baja fricción (F.5.5 / F.6): Los campos de carga manual utilizan etiquetas alineadas a la izquierda, pistas de formato explícitas y validación en tiempo real. Las contramedidas se presentan de a un paso por vez con edición en vivo (notas y temporizadores).

Technology for the System

  • Frontend: React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS — Prevents errors with medical units through strict typing and allows for high contrast (6:1) and offline visual alerts.
  • Charts and Telemetry: Apache ECharts or Recharts — Render time series of vital signs and flag signal gaps or stale data.
  • Backend: Python (FastAPI) + WebSockets — Transmits telemetry in real time with low latency, validates medical integrity (Pydantic), and allows for the integration of anomaly detection models.
  • Database: SQLite / IndexedDB (or PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB) — Stores time series using a local-first architecture to operate 100% offline on the spacecraft without relying on ground-based servers.
